**The Country of Night**

Just before half past four on the morning of January 17, 1994, the Northridge earthquake broke Los Angeles open. The shaking lasted perhaps twenty seconds; the darkness lasted longer. Transformers failed across the San Fernando Valley and beyond, and for miles the grid winked out, leaving a modern metropolis in a condition closer to the eighteenth century than the twentieth. People stumbled into streets. Generators coughed awake at hospitals. And then, in the hours that followed, a strange category of call began to reach police dispatchers, fire stations, and eventually the phones at the Griffith Observatory. Witnesses reported an enormous glowing object hanging over the darkened hills — a vast, silvery, smokelike presence in the sky that no one could account for. Some thought it must be gas burning somewhere underground. The staff at the observatory, when they finally heard the descriptions, reportedly needed no explanation at all. It was the Milky Way. People who had lived their entire lives beneath it were seeing, for the first time, the galaxy that contains their own city. The details of the story have blurred with retelling, and probably some of it is embellishment. But it has survived because it lands like a diagnosis: our lights had become so total that we had forgotten there was a galaxy on the premises.

That forgetting is now nearly complete, and it happened without anyone declaring it a policy. Nobody voted to erase the night. It was subtracted incrementally, lamp by lamp, screen by screen, subdivision by subdivision — a foreclosure conducted so gradually that it registered less as loss than as convenience. The dark didn't die. It got rezoned.

For most of human history, night was a hard border, and everyone knew where customs enforcement stood. After sundown, roads belonged to whoever carried a torch, which is why English cities employed link-boys whose whole profession was walking strangers safely through gloom they couldn't afford to dispel. Candles and lamp oil were expensive enough to budget like medicine, so households bent their lives around the sun's schedule in ways we can barely reconstruct: merchants opened at first light, courts adjourned before dusk, farmers banked their fires when darkness fell. Even our language remembers the enforcement. The word "curfew" descends from the French *couvre-feu* — cover the fire — the medieval instruction to smother your hearth when the ringing bell announced that legal night had begun. Every time a city orders its residents indoors, it is echoing an ordinance designed for an age when the alternative to going home was stumbling blind.

Then the borders softened. In 1807 a promoter named Frederick Winsor staged a gaslight demonstration along Pall Mall in London, and within two decades gas networks had threaded beneath the streets of London and Paris, lining thoroughfares with amber constellations that operated whether or not anyone could pay their own fuel bills. In September 1882, Edison's Pearl Street station switched on in lower Manhattan, serving about five dozen buildings in an arc of electric light, and the arithmetic changed permanently. Once illumination became cheap, the evening became a place you could *go* rather than a condition you endured. The very word "nightlife" barely predates the technology that made it possible. Cities earned nicknames like the City of Light partly as a compliment to their philosophers and partly as a plain description of what they looked like from the surrounding countryside. By the twentieth century, the invasion was essentially won; we just hadn't noticed what we'd conquered.

Here is what we surrendered, unknowingly, in the terms of the treaty. Before cheap light, historians discovered, human beings slept differently. Roger Ekirch, a historian at Virginia Tech, spent years combing through diaries, letters, depositions, and medical texts going back centuries, and found the same odd phrase recurring across languages and eras: "first sleep" and "second sleep." These weren't idioms. They described a schedule. People went to bed shortly after dark, slept deeply for a few hours, then woke naturally around midnight and remained tranquilly awake for an hour or more — praying, reviewing dreams for omens, reading by the fire, chatting with neighbors, or, according to some folkloric accounts, quietly committing petty crimes. Then came the second sleep, running until dawn. This wasn't a quirk of one culture. Ethnographers working with the Tiv people of Nigeria recorded a vocabulary that still divides the night into comparable intervals. And when researchers in the 1990s placed volunteers on a simulated long winter photoperiod — fourteen hours of darkness per day — the subjects drifted, within weeks, into precisely this biphasic pattern, complete with a peaceful interlude marked by measurable hormonal changes. Which suggests something disorienting: a great deal of what we medicalize as insomnia may simply be an ancient rhythm knocking politely on a door we've bricked shut. Waking at two in the morning is not a malfunction. It may be the most ancestral thing you do all day. What's new is the panic — the glance at the clock, the accounting of remaining hours, the cascading dread. The waking is old. Only the terror is modern.

Step away from a streetlight, deeper still, and another vanished country opens. Your vision changes hands entirely: cone cells retire, rod cells take over, and after half an hour of adaptation your sensitivity climbs by factors of ten thousand or more. Color drains asymmetrically — red abandons you first, which is why the night world reads in steely blues and greys — until you're navigating essentially in monochrome, the way the eye operated for most of mammalian history. Push further, to a place graded top marks on the astronomer's dark-sky scale, and you discover how absurd your former baseline was. There is the zodiacal light, a faint pyramid of dust-scattered sunlight standing over the western horizon. There is the gegenschein, a dim oval hovering opposite the sun. There is airglow — the upper atmosphere perpetually fluorescing — which means even the most "black" natural night is never black at all; the sky hums with chemistry directly above your head. Observers at such sites insist, reliably enough that cameras have sought confirmation, that the central band of the Milky Way grows bright enough to throw faint shadows onto pale ground. A fully dark-adapted human eye operates near the physical limits of the process: laboratory measurements suggest that only a handful of photons need strike a receptor for detection, and old naval tradition held that a candle flame could be spotted at distances beyond a mile on a clear night. You are carrying, wetted behind your eyelids, an instrument sensitive almost to individual quanta — and most of us deploy it, every night, in conditions closer to an operating theatre than to nature.

Because the dark, it turns out, is not empty space around the interesting stuff. It is habitat. Loggerhead and green sea turtle hatchlings emerge from Atlantic nests and steer for the sea by crawling toward the brighter, moonlit horizon over open water — which means beachfront floodlights become fatal misinformation, pointing generations of hatchlings inland toward highways. Songbirds migrate at night, some species navigating partly by star patterns, and tower lights draw them into fatal vortices. During New York's annual Tribute in Light, researchers found that the twin beams accumulated circling birds in the tens of thousands; when operators agreed to extinguish the lights for short periods whenever counts spiked, the skies cleared within minutes. Fireflies conduct their entire social life by targeted flashing, and skyglow drowns their vocabulary. Moths spiral themselves to exhaustion around bright lamps while spiders relocate webs underneath to harvest the confusion. Even corals may be affected: reef-building species coordinate spectacular simultaneous spawning by moonlight, and researchers worry that coastal light pollution is corrupting the calendar. Nor is the damage confined to wildlife — the World Health Organization's cancer agency classified shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen more than a decade ago. Meanwhile, the landmark 2016 world atlas of artificial sky brightness estimated that more than four-fifths of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, that the Milky Way is hidden from roughly a third of all people — including most Europeans and North Americans — at their homes, and that Singapore, taken as a whole, likely never experiences natural night anywhere on the island. We wrote these numbers down the way you inventory a deforestation.

Culture noticed first, as it usually does. Composers built an entire genre on the darker hours — the nocturne predates Chopin, but he made it his signature mood. Painters chased it too: in the 1870s, James McNeill Whistler exhibited his *Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket*, a nearly abstract scatter of sparks over a dark garden, and the critic John Ruskin accused him of flinging a pot of paint in the public's face. Whistler sued, won his symbolic farthing in damages, and considered himself vindicated. The poet's painter's problem was technical as much as spiritual: how do you render darkness without surrendering to flatness? Van Gogh attacked it head-on in Arles, boasting to his brother that he had painted a café terrace at night using no black at all — blues and violets and greens doing all the work — and wrote elsewhere that the night seemed to him more alive and more richly colored than the day. Months later, from the asylum window at Saint-Rémy, partly from imagination and memory, he produced the whorled explosion of *The Starry Night*. Generations have stood in front of it believing they were looking at fancy. They were mostly looking at documentation.

Then there is the quieter, intramural politics of night — who gets to have a morning. Chronotypes run partly in the blood, distributed unevenly across the population, and nearly every institution of work and school is tuned to the majority clock, which morally taxes the rest. We encode it in language: someone who rises early is praised as "up and about"; someone who sleeps until ten is vaguely suspect, as if lateness of waking implied lateness of character. And yet civilization maintains itself on circadian-stretched crews of bakers timing proofs in fluorescent pre-dawn kitchens, nurses coming off twelve-hour shifts, freight drivers rolling into distribution hubs, editors sweeping the overnight wire, and cleaners polishing lobbies so that daytime workers arrive to believe the building maintained itself. Every corner-store fruit display is evidence of a night shift you never saw. And inside your own skull, the dark-hours self performs its familiar degradation: executive function thins as the circadian trough arrives, so anxieties inflate at 3 a.m. with a vividness they will not survive breakfast. Clinicians know this pattern well. So, in fairness, did our ancestors — except they responded by getting up, banking a fresh fire, sitting with the strange alertness for a while instead of lying in the dark negotiating with catastrophe.

Zoom all the way out and the whole dispute reverses polarity. On Earth, night is a rotating privilege, granted and withdrawn with planetary mechanics. Step off the surface and the arrangement looks backwards: in orbit, sunlight returns every ninety minutes or so, and astronauts on the space station witness something like sixteen sunrises a day, sleeping through half of them. Beyond the atmosphere, the default condition of the cosmos is darkness — cold, photon-starved, punctuated by rare gravitational furnaces. When the Hubble telescope aimed weeks of accumulated exposure at what appeared to be an empty patch of sky, it recovered thousands of galaxies stacked in the depth. That is the correction worth keeping: darkness is not absence. It is distance. It is the medium through which everything you will ever see traveled to reach you.

None of this argues for abolishing streetlights. It argues for treating the dark the way conservationists learned to treat rivers — as infrastructure worth engineering around rather than through. Shield fixtures so light falls down instead of up, where it serves only moths and advertising agencies. Choose warmer spectra. Install motion sensors rather than all-night floods. Entire municipalities have done this — Flagstaff, Arizona pioneered such ordinances in the 1950s and became the world's first designated International Dark Sky City — and lost nothing but the orange dome above town. The biggest barrier isn't technology or cost. It's habit, and the mild superstitious belief that visible darkness signals neglect, that a properly managed property is always glowing, as if darkness were disorder rather than simply another registered state of the world.

So here is a small proposal, requiring neither legislation nor equipment. Somewhere in the next month, on a clear moonless evening, go outside for ten deliberate minutes. Don't photograph anything; your camera can't handle it anyway, and neither can your expectations, which have been trained on decades of sky glow. Give your eyes the half hour if you can spare it, or at least the stubborn ten. Find the Pleiades, that tiny frozen cluster, or the crooked W of Cassiopeia, or simply the cloudy seam of your own galaxy running overhead like spilled milk, which is what the Greeks concluded it was and what NASA's instruments spent billions confirming. If you live deep in a city you may fail completely — and that failure is data too, worth noticing the way you'd notice an odor or a noise. Because the strangest part of the Los Angeles story from 1994 is not that people saw something unfamiliar. It's that the unfamiliar thing had been over their heads every single clear night of their lives, patient as geology, enormous beyond metaphor, asking nothing. Nothing in the sky changed that January morning. Only the lights went out below, and something impossibly ordinary appeared.
